comparison_vs_a9.interpretation: Marginal gains on the already-overlapping DoS/Backdoor were paid for by clear regressions on Fuzzers, Shellcode, and Worms. Net attack-family and rare-class macro-F1 fell below A9. Binary is identical (router frozen).

classes_collapsed: Analysis: 0/677 predicted as Analysis (recall 0.000); 426 -> DoS, 128 -> Backdoor, 118 -> Exploits
Worms: recall collapsed 0.659 -> 0.273 (F1 0.331 -> 0.255); tiny support, overfit
Shellcode: precision collapsed 0.308 -> 0.194 (over-predicted; Fuzzers -> Shellcode 704); F1 0.440 -> 0.315
root_causes: Independent specialist encoder overfit: validation oracle macro-F1 0.5863 vs test 0.4747 (gap 0.1116).

Lost shared representation: attack-only training discarded the benign-informed joint A9 encoder (shaped by all 149,039 train rows + the binary task), which had helped Fuzzers/Shellcode/Worms; those classes regressed.

Class-weight over-pressure on rare classes: sqrt-inverse-frequency weights pushed Shellcode over-prediction (precision 0.31 -> 0.19) and did not save Worms recall (0.66 -> 0.27) -> rare macro fell to 0.285 (same RC5 pattern as A9.6).
Intrinsic RC1 overlap unchanged: Analysis/Backdoor/DoS/Exploits remain mutually confused; the specialist never predicts Analysis and uses Backdoor/DoS as low-precision dumping grounds.
Official-partition prior shift (RC4) amplifies the val->test gap: train/val benign 31.9% vs test 44.9%.
failure_diagnosis.oracle_vs_routed_interpretation: Oracle (teacher-forced on true attack rows) macro-F1 0.4747; routed end-to-end correctly-attributed rate 0.7193. The frozen A9 binary router reproduces A9 exactly (0.894488), so the routed cap is NOT the router -- the limitation is the specialist itself. Oracle is reported separately from routed and is not a deployment metric.

reasons: Seed42 fails both pre-registered screen gates (oracle 0.4747 < 0.515429 and below A9 0.5004; rare 0.2850 < 0.385669).
Running 3 seeds on a configuration that underperforms A9 on a single clean seed would waste compute and risk fishing for a lucky seed.
A9 remains stronger on attack-family and rare-class; it stays the accepted UNSW final baseline.
A9.9 is valuable as a diagnostic: it shows the independent attack-only encoder overfits and loses the shared representation -- directly informing A9.10.
